actions.justification: Mandatory first action: establish baseline vital signs and assess patient stability before any further workup or treatment.
Identify the patient's presenting complaint to guide differential diagnosis and determine which clinical guideline applies.
Perform a general status assessment to evaluate overall appearance, level of consciousness, and acute distress, informing initial triage and clinical decision-making.
Assess mental status as part of initial neurological evaluation - important baseline assessment for any patient presentation.
Evaluate cardiovascular status to identify any cardiac or hemodynamic concerns beyond the basic vitals already obtained.
Assess for potential infection sources to guide diagnosis and treatment planning during initial assessment phase.
Neurological assessment is a key component of the initial evaluation to identify any focal deficits or altered consciousness that may guide diagnosis and management.
Abdominal assessment is important to identify potential sources of pathology (e.g., peritonitis, organomegaly) not yet evaluated.
Hydration status assessment helps determine fluid balance and guides resuscitation decisions in the initial workup.
Comprehensive patient assessment to integrate all prior assessments and establish a working diagnosis given stable vitals at 45 minutes into the encounter.
Assess NIH Stroke Scale to screen for neurological deficits, as neurological status assessment is part of initial workup and stroke/TIA must be considered.
Assess pain level to characterize and quantify any pain complaints, which guides further diagnostic and treatment decisions.
Respiratory assessment not yet completed - important to evaluate breathing, lung sounds, and oxygenation status as part of comprehensive initial assessment.
Skin assessment not yet completed - evaluate for rashes, lesions, pallor, jaundice, or other findings that may guide diagnosis.
Musculoskeletal assessment not yet completed - evaluate for pain, swelling, or dysfunction that may be relevant to the chief complaint.
Evaluate for any organ dysfunction as part of the comprehensive initial assessment, even in a stable patient this is important to establish baseline.
Monitor urine output to assess renal perfusion and fluid status as part of the ongoing initial assessment.
Check baseline eGFR to establish renal function baseline, which guides further management decisions.
Establish IV access for potential medication administration, fluid resuscitation, or contrast if imaging is needed. Standard initial step after assessment.
Given the completed comprehensive assessment, specialist consultation is warranted to guide further diagnostic workup and management based on the identified clinical syndrome.
Patient has been thoroughly assessed; hospital admission ensures continued monitoring, further diagnostic workup, and appropriate treatment initiation pending specialist input.
